messages.author: 31e2049957f9d695
messages.subject: Analytic vs. Bootstrap Variance Estimation
parts:
Dear all,=20

I've got two problems with the variance estimations from my a Point =
Transect
Sampling data of a clustered population, where analytic estimations =
differ
strongly from those obtained by bootstrapping:

=20

1st Estimation of var(h(0)):

I know that constraints on the detection function have an influence on =
the
reliability of the analytic estimates of var(h(0)) (Buckland et al. =
2001:67),
so I checked that no constraints have caused estimates to be modified, =
but
nevertheless analytic and bootstrap estimations are very different:

Parameter | Method | Estimate | CV (%)

h(0) | Bootstrap(#999) | 0.67058E-02 | 26.19

h(0) | Analytic | 0.62081E-02 | 8.73

=20

=20

2nd Estimation of var(E(s)):

In a first step, I used the size biased regression method to estimated =
E(s).
Because the cluster size is fairly variable, I transformed z_i =3D =
ln(s_i) and
regressed g(y_i) on ln(s_i) as proposed by Buckland et al. (2001:75), =
but
again analytic and bootstrap estimations are very different:

Parameter | Method | Estimate | CV (%)

E(s) | Bootstrap(#999) | 12.096 | 29.55 =20

E(s) | Analytic | 18.512 | 11.855 | 8.57 =20

=20

Because the slope of the regression line isn't really significant I also
tried the mean of observed clusters to estimate E(s), with a similar =
result
as above:

Parameter | Method | Estimate | CV (%)

E(s) | Bootstrap(#999) | 18.570 | 20.32 =20

E(s) | Analytic | 18.512 | 11.57 =20

=20

=20

Does Anybody have an Idea which might explain the large differences =
between
analytic and bootstrap estimations?

Are there any assumptions I overlooked?

=20

=20

Kind regards,=20

Tim

=20

=20

--

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Analytic vs. Bootstrap Variance Estimation
parts:
Hi Tim, list,

By constraints I guess you mean monotonicity constraints. Looks like=20
removing those and running the bootstrap results in broadly similar=20
estimate of h(0) - the original (presumably with monotonicity=20
constraint) was 0.62E-2 and the mean of the bootstrapped (presumably=20
without monotonicity constraints) was 0.67E-2. So, you're getting a big=20
change in estimated variance with little change in estimated h(0). I=20
rather doubt it's the monotonicity constraint that's making such a large=20
difference - but I don't have any real basis for that statement. I=20
assume everything else about the model is the same (e.g., it's just one=20
key function and adjustment series in the bootstrap)? I wonder if you=20
get the same result if you fix the number of series adjustments, as I=20
guess you're allowing them to be selected in each bootstrap rep. What's=20
the sample size I wonder? It would also be helpful if you could somehow=20
provide a histogram of the data and the fitted detection function --=20
perhaps you could put that on a web site, or just post the distances if=20
there are not too many?

From what you've found with the variation in cluster size -- that it=20
has different variance in the bootstrap vs analytic when you estimate=20
variance using the cluster size regression, and similar when you just=20
use mean cluster size -- it seems clear that this is related to the=20
detection function issue above, so we'll need to clear that up first.

Cheers - Len

Hi Len, =20
yes, I mean monotonicity constraints - but I just wanted to point out =
that
this cannot be the problem (I checked that neither for the analytic nor =
the
bootstrap estimation any monotonicity constraints have caused estimates =
to be
modified).

I used the hazard-rate key function with number of series adjustments =
fixed
to zero (had the same idea as you ;-) ). For the bootstrapping procedure =
I
used the "Resample samples" option. I truncated the largest 10% of all
distances (no left truncation), sample size after truncation is 235 =
Point
Transects and 499 clusters.=20

The Cramer-von Mises family tests as well as the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
aren't significant, so that I assume the model fit is OK, but I put =
jpegs of
the detection function, the probability density function and the =
q-q-plot to
the following web address:
http://www.uni-forst.gwdg.de/~tritter1/distance_list/2011_04_12/ .

It seems clear to me, that the estimation of cluster size variance is =
related
to the detection function issue, when using the regression method (after =
all
it's a regression of g(y_i)). However, when I just use the mean size of
observed clusters, I do not understand why the detection function should =
be
related to this!?


Thanks a lot for your help,=20
Tim

without monotonicity constraints) was 0.67E-2. So, you're getting a big =

difference - but I don't have any real basis for that statement. I=20
assume everything else about the model is the same (e.g., it's just one=20
key function and adjustment series in the bootstrap)? I wonder if you=20
get the same result if you fix the number of series adjustments, as I=20

the sample size I wonder? It would also be helpful if you could somehow =

provide a histogram of the data and the fitted detection function --=20

From what you've found with the variation in cluster size -- that it=20

messages.subject: Re: AW: [DIST-SAMP] Analytic vs. Bootstrap Variance Estimation
parts:
Tim, with such large sample sizes, it's not clear to me what is going=20
wrong. However, your data are unusually long-tailed. I would be=20
inclined to truncate at say 20m or perhaps 25m, and see if the problem=20
persists. The hazard-rate model can produce some funny fits, especially=20
for point transect data, and especially when there are relatively large=20
numbers of detections close to the point. With greater truncation, you=20
may find that e.g. a half-normal model will fit well, and give more=20
stable results.

Steve Buckland
